reading: The same new cable put into walls of two kinds of house. Most new US homes, timber frame: the cable comes in through the top plate from the attic or ceiling space and drops straight down inside one stud bay, behind the board, to a socket near the floor; pulled through, quick. Most German homes, one plastered brick wall done two ways, both on one route: in at the top near the right side, down to a horizontal run some way below the top of the wall, across, down near the left corner, to a socket near the floor; a patch of broken plaster at a lower corner shows the brick beneath. On the surface, painted over: a duct screwed onto the plaster along the route and painted over; quick, the old wall unchanged and the duct in view. Cut in and plastered: a channel cut along the route, the cable laid and plastered over; slow, and the channel stays as a scar.
sourceNote: No numbers are drawn; no hours or days are given. The timber wall shows the common way to add a cable to a finished stud wall: from the attic or ceiling space through the top plate, down inside one stud bay, with no run across the studs (that would mean opening the board at every stud). The route in the brick walls follows the installation zones for concealed cables in DIN 18015-3 (BAUNETZ-DIN18015): horizontal runs in the upper zone, 15 to 45 cm below the ceiling (drawn at about 30 cm on a wall of about 2.5 m); vertical runs in zones 10 to 30 cm beside corners; the socket about 30 cm above the floor. The two routes differ because the walls are built differently. The walls are not drawn to scale. A duct screwed onto the surface is a regular, permitted way to run a cable; the middle wall shows it, not a repair of lesser standing. The labels describe general building practice for timber stud walls and plastered solid brick walls; the analogy is the owner's (transcript 2026-11-16-020) and the plan's analogy dictionary (plan-restart.md, rows 'Timber frame', 'Brick', 'Fresh paint on the facade': paint is a new part put on the old wall while the wall stays as it was). 'Most new US homes' / 'most German homes' are the owner's framing of the analogy, to be backed by the construction sources the plan names for section 0.
